lines.text: Where the Sahara meets the Sahel lies a land of ancient bones, a thousand-year empire and long, hard wars. This is the story of Chad.
About seven million years ago, an ape-like creature lived here. Its skull, found in Chad in 2001, may belong near the very root of the human line.
From the seven hundreds, the empire of Kanem, and later Bornu, ruled the lands around Lake Chad for more than a thousand years.
In the late eighteen hundreds a warlord, Rabih az-Zubayr, conquered Bornu, until the French killed him in battle in 1900.
That same year the French founded a post they called Fort-Lamy. Today it is the capital, N'Djamena.
Francois Tombalbaye would become Chad's first president, and be killed in a coup in 1975.
Hissene Habre would rule through the eighties, and much later be convicted of crimes against humanity.
Idriss Deby would seize power in 1990 and hold it for three decades, until he was killed fighting rebels.
In 1960 Chad won its independence from France, a vast landlocked country at the heart of the continent.
From 1978 Chad fought its northern neighbour Libya over the Aouzou Strip, in wars that lasted almost a decade.
After his father's death in 2021, Mahamat Deby took power, and was elected president in 2024.
In 2003 a pipeline opened to carry Chad's oil across Cameroon to the sea.
And in 2016 the Ennedi Massif, a sandstone plateau rich in ancient rock art, became a World Heritage Site.
From the oldest bones to the shores of Lake Chad, this land's story reaches back further than almost any other.
